summary: This work demonstrates a high-performance quantum interconnect between two superconducting modules using a 13.5 cm aluminum coaxial cable with $Q = 1.7 \times 10^6$ for the bus mode, enabling 98.2% single-photon state transfer fidelity and 92.5% Bell state fidelity via three-wave mixing through SNAIL couplers. By achieving such low transmission losses (0.2% infidelity contribution), the performance bottleneck has shifted to module-channel interface effects and Kerr nonlinearities, with successful transfer of high-dimensional binomially encoded logical states achieved.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing architectures require quantum interconnects between separate modules limited by transmission line losses. Existing implementations have been constrained by bus mode quality factors around $10^5$ in systems with bosonic error correction, necessitating improved channel designs to approach fundamental quantum capacity limits.
method: Two superconducting modules each containing a 3D cavity, transmon qubit, and SNAIL coupler are connected through a high-purity aluminum coaxial cable. Coherent state transfer is realized via pump-driven three-wave mixing with Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{BS}^{j} = g_j(e^{-i\Delta_j t}\hat{a}_j^\dagger \hat{b} + e^{i\Delta_j t}\hat{a}_j \hat{b}^\dagger)$, achieving complete photon swap in 0.8 μs with coupling strength $g_{BS}/2\pi \approx 0.5$ MHz. Quantum process tomography and Wigner tomography characterize transfer fidelities across single-photon and multi-photon binomial encodings.
result: Single-photon state transfer achieves 98.2% process fidelity per transfer and Bell state fidelity of 92.5%; binomial logical state transfer reaches 94.8% fidelity ($F_2/F_1$). Error budget analysis shows transmission line losses contribute only 0.2% infidelity, with primary constraints from cavity decoherence (0.5%), SNAIL dephasing (0.3%), ac-Stark shifts (0.6%), and cross-Kerr interactions (0.2–0.3%). Simulations reveal kHz-level self-Kerr coefficients substantially degrade higher-photon-number states, imposing a fundamental limitation for increased capacity.
